idiom_name: actor-isolated reorder window + ordered AsyncStream output
implementation_notes: Swift's structured concurrency (TaskGroup, async let) preserves no order among concurrently produced values and the standard library has no reorder stage, so the resequencer is an actor: an actor-isolated dictionary keyed by sequence number, an expected cursor and a deadline driven by ContinuousClock or Task.sleep. Delivery into an AsyncStream keeps the observer side ordered because the stream hands values to its iterator in the order they were yielded, so the actor should only yield once the cursor has advanced past a hole; the continuation's buffering policy is where the capacity bound lives.
pitfalls: Actors are reentrant at suspension points: if accept awaits before updating the cursor, another call can interleave and deliver the same sequence number twice - mutate the window synchronously and suspend only for the yield.
TaskGroup results arrive in completion order and awaiting them in creation order does not restore it; only the sequence number (or an actor holding the cursor) defines order.
An AsyncStream continuation with an unbounded buffering policy defeats any capacity bound the resequencer sets; pair them or the reorder window silently relocates into the stream buffer.
